item.title: Why We Need To Pay More Attention To Ugoccie - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Born in Abia State, educated there, and later working as an on-air personality in Anambra, her voice travelled across Imo and Enugu through radio.

item.title: Ms Gideon Just Joined the Chat - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Ms Gideon is clear that her music will always carry a sonic essence shaped by her roots and Namibian heritage. She writes from her memory of growing up in Namibia, from personal encounters, from real conversations.

item.title: Started With A Game: How One Brutal Result Changed The Way Tosin Engaged The Game - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Before the ring light, before the followers, Tosin was quieter than her audience might expect.

item.title: Standing Between Violence and Silence: Hillary Leong’s Fight for Women and Children - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Some people arrive in advocacy through policy, profession, or public pressure. For Hillary Leong, the path began much earlier through survival, outside institutions, formal campaigns, or public recognition.

item.title: Ethiopian Traditional Hair and Skin Routine (Weyba Tis) - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: The secret ingredients? Pure, homemade butter and sometimes honey. They apply this everywhere, even to the hair and the private parts. Then, they use a special wood called Weyba. It’s placed in the hole with a very dim fire so it doesn't burn, but creates a thick, aromatic smoke.

item.title: Inside “tHERapy”: The Lagos Play Forcing Audiences to Confront Trauma, Silence and SurvivalInside Therapy - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Tosin’s latest project, Therapy, is a one-woman play written and performed by Oladotun Olagbadebo, with Adeyemi as Director.

item.title: Henry Akrong: Everything Else Came First. Art Came Lasting. - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Henry Akrong speaks about art with very little mythology. There is no dramatic story of early certainty, no carefully packaged narrative about always knowing exactly who he wanted to become. If anything, he describes his creative life as something that was always present, but not always fully acknowledged.

item.title: The Price of Experiencing Nigeria: What Rising Costs Are Doing to Tourism - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: The irony is that Nigeria’s strongest tourism appeal has never really depended on conventional tourist attractions. People do not come only for monuments or historic landmarks. They come because Nigerian cities have become cultural experiences in themselves.

item.title: Why Kigali Is Becoming a Serious Player in Africa’s Creative Future - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Kigali has grown differently from the continent’s louder cultural capitals. Its presence has been gradual, built with less noise and more intention. Yet that quietness is precisely why the city is beginning to attract more serious attention.

item.title: The Animator Pushing Nigerian Storytelling Forward: Willy Kanga - Draft Africa - African Storytellers
item.description: Before audiences knew him as Willy Kanga, he was William, an architecture student trying to create a social media identity that sounded memorable enough to stay.
